pages.content:
Get ready to start your web development journey - right here, right now.


**By the end of this course, you will:**

- Understand what HTML is and why it's the backbone of every website 
- Create your first webpage using easy-to-follow steps 
- Master essential HTML tags for content, images, links, lists, tables, and forms 
- Discover the importance of semantic HTML to create well-structured, accessible pages 
- Learn SEO basics to help your web pages perform well on search engines 


**Why Learn HTML?**

- HTML is the starting point for every web developer. Whether your goal is to become a blogger, programmer, or entrepreneur, understanding HTML gives you a strong foundation for building websites and applications.
- No prior experience is required to get started.




**How This Course Works**

- Structured in short, focused lessons so you can learn at your own pace 
- Includes real-world examples to help you apply what you learn immediately 
- Designed with beginners in mind, using clear explanations and simple language 
- Provides ready-to-use code snippets you can copy, modify, and test

pages.title: Definition and Purpose of HTML
pages.content:
- HTML stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. 
- It is the standard language used to create and organize content on the web. HTML tells your browser what each part of a web page means and how it should appear.
- Think of HTML as the blueprints and skeleton of a website - it defines the essential structure and parts of a page.




---

**Why Do We Use HTML?**

- To Structure Web Content : HTML organizes text, images, links, headings, tables, and other content into a format your browser can display.
- To Provide Meaning : It not only lays out content but also gives it semantic meaning, helping browsers and assistive technologies understand the purpose of elements on the page.
- To Enable Web Browsers to Render Pages : Without HTML, browsers wouldn’t know how to show content - HTML is essential for displaying anything on the web.

---

**What’s Next?**

Now that you know what HTML is and why it’s so important, let’s explore the **Role of HTML in Web Development** - understanding how HTML works with other technologies like CSS and JavaScript to build modern websites.


It belongs at the beginning of the document, before the `<html>` element. It does not render visible content.

pages.title: body Tag
pages.content:
In this section, you'll learn about the `<body>` tag — the part of an HTML document that contains all the visible content of a webpage.

---

**What is `<body>`?**\
The `<body>` element holds everything that the user actually sees when they visit a webpage in their browser.

This includes:
* Headings
* Paragraphs
* Images
* Links
* Lists
* Buttons
* And all other visible elements

If you think of a webpage like a theater play:
* The `<body>` is the backstage setup.
* The `<body>` is the stage where the action happens.

Everything you want to display on your site should go inside the `<body>` tag.

---

**Why Is `<body>` Important?**\
Without the `<body>` tag, your webpage would be blank. It's the main section where you create your page's layout, content, and structure that users will interact with.

pages.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
pages.content:
When you create a link, you're giving the browser directions to a new destination. Just like with real-world directions, you can give a full, complete address or a simpler, partial one. This is the difference between an **absolute path** and a **relative path**.

---

Let's use a simple analogy: giving a friend directions.

**Absolute Path (The Full Address):**

- Imagine telling your friend, "Go to **1600 Amphitheatre Parkway, Mountain View, CA**." This is a complete address. No matter where your friend is starting from, they can find that exact location.
- In HTML, an **absolute path** is a link to another website. It always includes the full URL, starting with `https://` or `http://`.

**Example:** `Google`

---

**Relative Path (The Local Directions):**

- Imagine telling your friend, "Go to the **coffee shop next door**." This is a partial address. It only works if your friend is starting from your current location.
- In HTML, a **relative path** is a link to another file *within your own website*. The path is relative to the location of the current file.

**Example:** `About Us`

The browser will look for a file named `about.html` in the **same folder** as the page you are currently on.

pages.title: Anchor Links - Navigating within the Same Page
pages.content:
So far, you've learned to create links that take you to new pages. But what if you have a very long page and want to create a "Table of Contents" that jumps to different sections?


- That's where **anchor links** come in. An anchor link allows you to navigate to a specific spot on the **same page**, without a page reload.
- Think of it like a table of contents in a book. You don't have to turn to a new book; you just jump to a new section within the same book.

---
To make an anchor link work, you need two key parts:
1. **The Destination:** You must give the element you want to jump to a unique name using the `id` attribute.
 * `id` stands for "identifier."
 * **Example:** `Section 1`
2. **The Link:** You create a regular anchor tag, but the `href` attribute starts with a `#` symbol, followed by the name of the destination `id`.
 * **Example:** `Go to Section 1`

The `#` symbol is the key. It tells the browser, "Don't go to a new page. Instead, look for an element with this `id` on the page you're currently viewing."

pages.title: HTML footer Tag
pages.content:
The `<footer>` tag is a semantic HTML element that defines the bottom section of a webpage or a section within a page.

**What is a `<footer>`?**\
Think of it as the closing section of your document. It typically contains information about the author, copyright data, contact information, and secondary navigation links. It's where you put all the "wrap-up" content that a visitor might need after they've finished reading the main content.

---

**Key Features and Use Cases**

* **Copyright Info:** The most common use is to display a copyright notice (e.g., `© 2024 Your Website`).
* **Contact Details:** You can include links to social media profiles or contact forms.
* **Secondary Navigation:** It's a great place for links that are not part of the main navigation, such as a Privacy Policy or Terms of Service.
* **Reusability:** Like the `<footer>` tag, a webpage can have multiple `<footer>` tags. You can use one at the very bottom of the page and another at the end of a specific article or section.

pages.title: HTML Tables
pages.content:
Tables in HTML help you organize data into rows and columns, making information like schedules, lists, or comparisons easy to read.

**The Main Table Tags**

- `<table>`: The container that holds the entire table
- `<table>`: Creates a row within the table (Table Row)
- `<table>`: Defines a regular cell that contains data (Table Data)
- `<table>`: Creates a header cell - these are bold and centered to label columns or rows (Table Header)

---

**How Tables Work**

pages.title: Form - name, value, and placeholder
pages.content:
You've learned that the `<form>` tag is a container for all the interactive parts of your form. Now, let's look at the three essential attributes that allow you to put data *into* that container and send it to a server.

* The `name` attribute is the most important one. It acts as the unique identifier for a piece of data. When you submit a form, the `name` is the 'label' that tells the server what it's receiving. For example, if you have a field for a user's name, you would give it a `name` like `"username"`.

* The `value` attribute holds the actual data for that `name`. For a text field, the `value` is the text the user types. For a button, it's the text on the button itself.

* The `placeholder` attribute is a short hint that appears inside the input field. It's a helpful cue for the user (e.g., "Enter your email here") that disappears as soon as they start typing. The `placeholder` is for user experience only and is not sent to the server as data.

Together, `name` and `value` are the fundamental pair that a browser uses to communicate with a server. The `placeholder` is an optional helper that makes the form easier to use.

pages.title: textarea - Multiline Input
pages.content:
- You've learned to create single-line inputs for things like names, emails, and passwords using the `<textarea>` tag. But what if you need to give a user a large space to write a full message or comment?
- For that, you'll use the `<textarea>` element.
- The `<textarea>` tag is designed specifically for collecting long, free-form text that can span multiple lines. Unlike the self-closing `<textarea>` tag, the `<textarea>` element is a block-level element that requires a separate closing tag: `<textarea>`.
- This allows the user to type as much as they need, and it often comes with a built-in resizing handle in the corner.

---

Here are the key attributes you'll use with it:

* `name`: Just like with `<textarea>`, this is the most important attribute. It provides the unique identifier for the data, telling the server what this block of text is.
* `rows`: This attribute sets the visible height of the text area in rows (or lines). For example, `rows="5"` will make the text area five lines tall.
* `cols`: This attribute sets the visible width of the text area in characters. For example, `cols="50"` will make the text area approximately 50 characters wide.
* `placeholder`: This attribute works just like it does on other inputs, providing a short hint inside the text area until the user starts typing.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: textarea - Multiline Input demonstrates a core HTML concept. Use valid structure, semantic elements, and accessible attributes where applicable.

  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>textarea - Multiline Input</title>
</head>
<body>
  <textarea name="feedback" rows="5" placeholder="Share your feedback"></textarea>
</body>
</html>
